messages.text: just feel like i'm running on fumes this week, y'know? like i'm doing all the things but not really present for any of it.

It sounds like you’re feeling drained and going through the motions without much connection to what you’re doing. That can happen when stress builds and energy doesn’t get replenished. Can you recall what’s been taking the most out of you lately, or what’s been missing that normally helps you feel grounded?
eh, just work stuff mostly. you know how it is — traffic, bad tippers, the usual. adds up after a while.

Yeah, those everyday frustrations can pile up and leave you feeling depleted. When there’s no real break, even small stressors start feeling heavier. Have you found any quick ways to recharge during your day, even for just a few minutes?

yesterday was wild — got a call for a airport pickup at 5 am, right? so i'm already tired, haven't slept well cause the dog was barking all night. get to the terminal, guy's luggage is oversized, so i have to pay the fee or he won't let it in the car. then he argues with me the whole 45 minutes to downtown, says i took a wrong turn twice even though gps said otherwise. gets out, leaves a one-star and no tip. felt like i got kicked in the teeth before 7 am.

That sounds incredibly frustrating and exhausting, especially when you were already running on little sleep. Being treated unfairly like that can leave you feeling drained and powerless. How have you been processing that experience since it happened?
ah, it's not that big a deal in the grand scheme. just one of those days, happens all the time. i mean, i've had worse.

It’s true that tough days happen, but repeated experiences like that can still chip away at your energy and mood over time. Sometimes we minimize them to keep moving forward, but they can still weigh on us. Would you be open to exploring ways to release some of that stress before it builds up?
you know what... i said it was just work, but that’s not really true. i’ve been carrying this heavy feeling all week, and it’s not just the bad rides. it’s something going on with my son.

It sounds like what’s affecting you runs much deeper than the work stress, and involves concern for your son. That can bring a whole different level of emotional weight. Do you want to share what’s been happening with him so we can talk it through?

yeah... it's about my son. he's 14. school called last week — there's some kind of incident, accusations from another student. i don't even know what really happened yet. just that they're saying he did something, and now everything's in motion and i don't know who to believe or what to do.

That must feel overwhelming, especially without clear information and with the stakes so high for your son. Uncertainty in situations like this can fuel anxiety and make you feel powerless. Have you been able to speak directly with him about what happened, or get more details from the school yet?

so the call came friday afternoon. vice principal said there was an “incident” involving my son and another student — something about him being aggressive, pushing, maybe threats? they wouldn’t give details over the phone, just that it’s under review and i need to come in monday. i asked to speak to my son, but they said he was already dismissed. that felt off. 

i finally got him to talk saturday morning. he says it’s blown out of proportion — that the other kid was messing with his bag, he pushed him away, said “back off” — but nothing about threats. he says the kid fell and made a scene. but now the parents are saying he’s been bullying their son for weeks. never heard any of this before. 

we went to the meeting monday. they were calm but distant, kept saying “we’re just gathering facts,” but i could tell they already made up their minds. wanted me to agree to some behavioral plan, like he’s a problem kid. i said no — not without seeing evidence. they didn’t like that. now i’m waiting to hear back, and every minute feels like i’m failing him somehow.

It sounds like you’re caught in a situation where you don’t feel heard, and you’re trying to protect your son while getting to the truth. That combination of conflicting accounts and the school’s stance could understandably leave you feeling anxious and defensive. Right now, what would help you most — clarity on the facts, guidance on advocating for him, or support in managing your own stress through this?

i don't even know. part of me says stand my ground — he's not a violent kid, i know that. but what if i'm wrong? what if i'm just seeing what i want to see? and if i push too hard, do i make him look more defiant? but if i back down too fast, does that tell him i don't believe in him? feels like no matter what i do, i lose.

It’s completely understandable to feel stuck between protecting your son and wanting to be fair in how you see the situation. Those doubts can be heavy, especially when there’s no clear evidence yet. You might focus on gathering as much information as possible while keeping open communication with him, so your actions show both support and commitment to truth. Would you like to think together about questions or steps that can help clarify the facts?
yeah, i think that could help. i don't even know what to ask that won't make me look like i'm attacking them. what questions would actually get me the truth without making things worse?

You could ask for specifics about the timeline, witness accounts, and any documented evidence, like reports or camera footage, in a calm, non-confrontational way. Clarifying how the school defines terms like “bullying” or “aggression” can also help you understand their perspective. You might frame questions as wanting to partner with them to help your son succeed, which keeps the tone collaborative. Would you like me to help you phrase those questions in a way that feels neutral but still gets answers?

that actually helps. i was spinning, thinking it was either fight or surrender. but asking questions like that — calm, clear — feels like something i can do. yeah, if you could help me word it right, that'd be good. don't want to sound aggressive, but i need to know what really happened.

You could start with, “I want to understand the situation clearly so I can support my son appropriately — could you walk me through exactly what happened from your perspective?” Then, “Are there written reports or witness statements I could review?” and “Can you explain how you determined this might be bullying, and what criteria you use?” These keep the focus on facts, not accusations, and signal you’re willing to work with them while staying informed. Would you like me to also suggest a closing statement that reinforces your commitment to fairness and your son’s well-being?
yeah, that’d be good. thanks — really. i was stuck in my head about this, and now it feels like there’s a path forward.

You could close with something like, “My goal is to ensure a fair and thorough process that supports all students involved, including my son. I appreciate your willingness to share information, and I want to work together toward a resolution that promotes safety and understanding.” This reinforces that you’re reasonable, cooperative, and focused on fairness. How are you feeling right now after talking through these next steps?
relieved. not fixed, but — clearer. like i can breathe again. felt like i was drowning in guesses and fear, and now i’ve got something real to do. that helps.

I’m glad you feel more grounded and have some concrete steps to focus on. That sense of direction can make uncertainty easier to handle. Remember, you’re doing your best to protect and support your son while seeking the truth. Do you want to check in again after you’ve had that conversation with the school?
yeah, i'd like that. not sure when it'll happen — they haven't called me back yet — but having someone to check in with? that helps. makes it feel less like i'm alone in this.

I’m here to help you process and plan whenever you need. Waiting without updates can be tough, so it might help to keep notes on any thoughts or questions that come up in the meantime. That way you’ll be ready when the school contacts you. Would you like a few quick ideas for how to manage the stress during this waiting period?
it's not just the not knowing — though that's bad enough. it's the feeling that every second i'm not doing something, i'm failing him. is that normal? or am i overreacting?

That feeling is common for parents in situations like this, because the stakes feel so personal and urgent. It doesn’t necessarily mean you’re overreacting — it’s a sign of how deeply you care. Sometimes doing nothing is actually part of the process, especially when waiting for the next step is unavoidable. Would you like me to share ways to reframe that “doing nothing” so it feels less like failing?
thanks. yeah, that helps. i needed to hear that. it's not that i want to do nothing — i just need to know that staying calm and waiting isn't the same as giving up on him.

Exactly — staying calm and waiting can be an active choice that protects your energy and readiness to advocate when the time comes. You’re conserving mental strength so you can respond clearly and effectively. That’s a form of support, not surrender. Would you like me to outline a simple plan to help you keep that focus while you wait?
yeah, that makes sense. i can work with that. if you've got a plan, i'm open to it.

You could start with short daily check-ins with yourself: note your emotional state, any new questions, and small steps you can take to prepare. Build brief grounding routines—like a walk, deep breathing, or listening to something calming—to keep your stress level manageable. Keep a list of what you want to ask or clarify when the school contacts you, so you feel ready rather than reactive. Would you like me to help you create a few grounding exercises tailored to your day’s rhythm?
thanks. really. i came in feeling like i was drowning and now i’ve got a plan, some tools, and a way to breathe. that means a lot.

I’m glad you’re leaving here feeling more steady and equipped to handle what’s ahead. Remember, caring for yourself is part of caring for your son. You can come back anytime you need to recharge or regroup. Would you like me to check in next time on how the school conversation went?
yeah, that'd be good. i'll reach out, but if you check in, even better. helps me stay on track.

I’ll be ready to follow up and see how things are progressing when you reach out. In the meantime, keep using your plan and grounding tools so you feel prepared, not pressured. You’re handling a tough situation with thought and care. Take care of yourself tonight.
